rv.q: Vogel's nuanced exploration of her own family sets the stage for a profound and humorous new American play.
That’s what “Mother Play” is, a balm that comes in cardboard boxes and packing tape.
Lange is magnificent, especially in this production’s most moving scene: a long passage that the script calls the Phyllis Ballet.

It's a measure of the superb acting in Tina Landau's production that you easily believe the middle-aged Keenan-Bolger and Parsons as high-schoolers, just as you do the 74-year-old Lange as a woman in her 30s.

Jessica Lange plays a hapless, helpless and hopelessly bad single mother in Paula Vogel’s bluntly titled “Mother Play,” a funny and affecting but slight and fragmentary drama depicting Ms. Lange’s Phyllis and her tortured relationship with her son and daughter across several decades.
Lange is magnificent in her depiction of a woman who, across the decades, can’t quite reconcile what her life or her children have become.
That cleverness, however, has a domineering quality.
While Jessica Lange gobbles up the meaty role of Mother and tragic experiences befall the family, the play resolves with eye-rolling sentimentalism.
Mother Play isn’t quite specific or emotionally searing enough to live beyond its admittedly alluring reference points.
Paula Vogel's 'Mother Play' is a memory piece that feels less like theater than like an extended therapy session, despite Jessica Lange's commanding presence.
Mother Play showcases powerhouse performances by Jessica Lange, Jim Parsons, and Celia Keenan-Bolger.
In any event, Vogel’s play and players merit a visit to the Helen Hayes.
One can even imagine who Phyllis, and the other “mothers” like her, might have become had they defied societal expectations.

“Mother Play” is not as great as plays Paula Vogel has written in the past – perhaps not as great as she might be able to make it in time – but under Tina Landau’s direction, it is a mesmerizing production, albeit not always easy to watch.
In the end, “Mother Play” encourages us to better understand and appreciate both kinds, and the people we spend them with.
In its excellence, her work in “Mother Play” recalls what she did on stage as Mary Tyrone in “Long Day’s Journey into Night” in 2016.
It is Lange who stands at the center, giving a performance that throughout is full of nuance as she portrays this complicated mess of a woman.
The play is full of moments like this where, like it or not, we see our lives displayed on that stage.
Some creative choices don’t pay off, but Vogel’s latest hits the emotional beats it needs to, and is certainly a powerful reminder to call your mom now and then.
But mostly, Mother Play feels a cold, airless, and puzzling tundra to orienteer—despite the can-this-be-happening electricity of watching Jessica Lange perform on stage.

Mother Play, though based on Vogel’s own life, is at her most schematic, more an outline barely fleshed out with lots of details rather than the intense emotional revelations of her earlier works such as How I Learned to Drive and Indecent.
Mother Play covers too much ground without providing enough emotional depth to overcome its familiarities.
However, in many ways Mother Play seems like a work-in-progress only partially saved by Lange’s brilliant performance.
The scene that followed was, by far, the most brilliant moment of Mother Play.
As a result, Mother Play presents a blinkered portrait of an interesting but flawed heroine.
Mother Play touches on familiar issues to which many Broadway playgoers will relate, even if they sometimes smack of contrivance.
Lange steals every scene she is in, and she makes everyone better around her, proving that she is a giving actress.
And, of course, that play turned out to be Mother Play.

cn.t: Vogel's semi-autobiographical family drama earns praise for Lange's commanding performance and bold stylistic choices, but critics find the play itself uneven, with some calling it emotionally underpowered and overly therapeutic despite its humor and inventive staging.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's smallest houses (597 seats) and one of its newest, built in 2015 as Second Stage's permanent home. The intimate scale means excellent sightlines from nearly every seat, though the modern design prioritizes function over grandeur.

acc.note: Elevator from lower lobby to Mezzanine. LOOP system for t-coils and cochlear implants.

vr.q: Jessica Lange is absolutely incredible and the show is really funny even goofy at points and so heartfelt but also touches on a lot of really important and painful issues
The performances in this play are incredible, and nuanced, and feel, for lack of a better term, very real.
